33834e0ba850.text: A neuron spikes on crossing threshold, resets to −60 mV and remains refractory for 1 ms. The 160 PNs project randomly to 1,000 KCs with connection probability 0.05, about eight PN inputs per KC. Incoming weights total 800 nS per KC. One APL receives from every KC and inhibits every KC; each direction uses 30 nS connections. Five MBONs, one per KT gas, receive from all KCs and inhibit one another.

608660f8a0d5.text: The KC spike trace x rises by 0.1 per spike and decays with a 10 ms time constant. Active KCs raise their thresholds toward 0 mV; sufficiently quiet KCs relax toward −60 mV. This balances responsiveness and sparsity rather than fixing the active fraction in advance.

4777e6cf2505.text: Only KC→MBON synaptic weights learn. Pre- and postsynaptic traces decay over 5 ms; spike pairs increase weight by up to 0.025 nS. Both temporal orders potentiate, unlike classical asymmetric STDP.

f5842d349e48.text: After every training presentation, each KC’s five outgoing weights are normalized to a total of 10 nS, with individual weights within 0–10 nS. Strengthening one output therefore reduces the relative strength of the others.

521c89c94084.text: During training, the correct-class teacher starts 1 ms after odor onset and drives its MBON; mutual inhibition suppresses competitors. 0867124776c9.text: A biological response can only be read after sample molecules reach the cells and emitted light reaches the detector. We separated these steps to ask which part of the proposed geometry could limit a usable signal: optical collection, excitation leakage, gas distribution or transport through the liquid.

dbecac648164.text: A shared detector must collect fluorescence while preserving information about which well produced it. We therefore varied optical geometry and tracked source and detector locations separately. In the sensitivity plots, compare collection with spatial variation; in the mixing matrix, follow one LED row across source wells to distinguish the intended contribution from optical crosstalk.

3271de4cf276.text: Frequency tagging alone cannot remove excitation light arriving at the same modulation frequency as fluorescence. Filter selection therefore asks how much unwanted current can be removed without sacrificing too much useful signal. Read the spectral curves first, then compare integrated currents and signal-to-noise estimates under the same assumed sources.

04cdb9c4eff8.text: An inlet flow rate does not tell us when each well receives the sample or whether delivery is even. We compared chamber geometry and flow conditions using the same inlet concentration step. The maps locate delayed regions; the surface curves show their timing and spatial spread, so both arrival speed and differences between wells inform the operating choice.

013640101d07.text: Gas reaching a well is only the first delivery step: bottom-attached cells remain separated from it by liquid. We next varied liquid depth and diffusivity, then added a membrane to the transport model. Read the depth comparison before the membrane sweep to see whether a proposed barrier adds delay to a path already limited by the liquid.

4ad14c7ea0b5.text: Overlapping sensor responses make a useful test of sparse expansion: can a larger neural representation make gas identity easier to read? The circuit diagram separates that representation from the learned output, and distinguishes the teacher used during training from the information available during testing. Those distinctions guide the later layerwise comparisons.

031c7423a074.text: Before comparing learning rules, the measurements must be represented consistently without using test-set information. The workflow follows an exposure from sensor features to neural input; the gas-by-sensor heatmap then shows which response patterns overlap. This connects the encoding choices to the later classwise errors.

01b463562dca.text: Expansion, inhibition and readout learning perform different jobs in the model. We kept those stages explicit so that a classification error could later be traced to the representation or to the rule that learns from it, rather than treating the network as a single unexplained classifier.

ea8af57a886a.text: The split determines the question a score can answer. Mixing exposures across days tests separation within the sampled collection, whereas holding out whole days tests transfer to different collection conditions. We keep those comparisons distinct from the later chronological UCI analysis and fit preprocessing within the training partition.

af6992ca0c73.text: An overall score can conceal a class that the network repeatedly confuses. We first examine the confusion matrix against the earlier sensor-response heatmap, then use spike rasters to follow an example through the network. The matrix describes the error pattern; the rasters help interpret how a particular decision develops.

145ae083135b.text: A high pooled score is less useful if the classifier relies on conditions shared by the training and test days. We therefore kept measurement days intact and compared classifiers under the same split question. Read the random and unseen-day bars as a change in evaluation conditions before interpreting the drop as a particular physical drift mechanism.

069a5bba4575.text: We also asked whether the chosen setting depended on a narrow parameter choice. The one-factor sweep changes one setting at a time around the earlier reference, so departures from the dashed line identify parameters worth controlling. This comparison concerns sensitivity of that run, rather than independent confirmation of a new optimum.

973f073b04e7.text: The classwise errors leave two possibilities: useful information was lost upstream, or the learned output failed to use information still present. We trained conventional probes at successive representations on a common split. Compare the layer scores first, then the learned MBON output, to locate the loss within this diagnostic experiment.

f4154d0d6a1b.text: The layer diagnosis motivated a more focused comparison in which the representation stays fixed and only the readout rule changes. The offline bars ask whether averaging, error-dependent updates or a conventional linear classifier recover more of the same KC information; they do not compare different upstream encoders.

3c1447428ff1.text: Unseen-day evaluation cannot by itself describe how sensor responses evolve over a long deployment. We therefore used the separate UCI batches to examine response gain, its shared and gas-dependent components, and the resulting classification loss. Read the sensor traces before the decomposition: a correctable common shift need not describe every sensor–gas pair.

40d7f53db1ed.text: To separate classification within a batch from transfer between batches, we compared where the training data came from and whether test concentrations were covered. The curves should therefore be read as different coverage conditions, not interchangeable estimates of one drift penalty.

e634bd84f7ff.text: The shared drift components suggest a practical question: can measurements of one reference gas help classify the others? We compared that correction with global and per-sample normalization. The gas-specific comparator uses additional information, so its bar provides context rather than the expected outcome of an ethanol-only procedure.

e39cf32009b7.text: A deployed classifier may encounter a gas that was absent from its initial training. We used a sequential-learning run to ask whether learning the added class disrupts previously learned classes. Read the before-and-after fractions for the old and new gases together: success on the new class alone would hide forgetting.

6ec3aa8877ed.text: Receptor selection needs functional response evidence before a structural score can be useful. We began with published receptor–odorant measurements and retained their identities in the response matrix. Its rows and columns define the benchmark; holding out receptors or chemical groups then asks different questions about extending beyond the observed combinations.

7ffd703bb120.text: The first cycle connects candidate choice to a prediction test. We compare published responses to the selected mold-related and control panels, then ask which molecular and receptor features help predict held-out measurements. Read the panel differences as a selection criterion and the matched ablations as a test of added information, rather than evidence that a designed mutation works.

76ca5d9e1154.text: A retained baseline provides a reference for asking whether a richer description of an odorant adds useful information. The following studies test measured vibrations, computed modes and a learned molecular representation. Each comparison keeps its eligible compounds and evaluation folds matched, so a change in dataset coverage is not mistaken for a feature benefit.

f10e6559dafe.text: Measured IR offers a description of molecular vibrations beyond the original descriptors, but it may also overlap with size-related information. We compared adding spectra with removing molecular weight or the broader size-feature group. Read each variant against its matched baseline separately for chemical and receptor holdouts; a gain in one task need not transfer to the other.

85b9cd89c415.text: Computed harmonic modes let us test a different vibration representation and whether its dimensionality obscures useful signal. We compared frequency-based EVA, intensity-weighted computed IR, fold-contained compression and random-feature controls. The second figure retrains measured and computed alternatives on their shared compounds, separating that comparison from results obtained on the larger eligible cohorts.

38cefe7f4d5f.text: A representation learned from odor descriptions might capture chemical relationships missing from hand-built features, but receptor-response prediction is a different task. We therefore transferred frozen OpenPOM features without treating pretraining as receptor validation. Compare the matched model variants first, then the paired gain intervals to judge whether the apparent changes are distinguishable from uncertainty.

be03ec4797cb.text: Extending a fly-trained model to another species requires more than recognizing similar sequences. We tested direct response prediction against mosquito measurements and separately compared sequence similarity with similarity of functional profiles. The scatter tests agreement of predictions with observations; the method comparison asks whether local sequence matching supplies a useful ranking signal.

492918a05620.text: Static docking samples one receptor conformation; receptor motion might alter the accessible poses and their ranking. In the separate reference complex, we compared static and trajectory-derived ensembles against a published functional panel. The ranking plot tests predictive usefulness, while the trajectory diagnostics show how uncertain or drifting structural regions qualify that interpretation.

aa8ba98f7ea0.text: Docking places an odorant in a pocket without showing how it arrives there. We next varied starting locations and molecular availability to distinguish finding the receptor from entering its pocket. Follow distance and pocket contacts for the same molecule together; an approach or surface encounter does not satisfy the sustained-entry criterion.

We guided entrance distances toward the unbound reference and monitored the odorant independently. In the paired panels, reduced geometry error shows that guidance affected the receptor; ligand distance and persistence after bias removal test the separate question of release.

7f33ead4578b.text: A corridor that admits a point probe may still be blocked for an odorant with finite size and orientation. We therefore progressed from empty-space maps to whole-ligand placement and flexible pulling. Read target motion separately from actual ligand motion, then use the clash scans and waiting comparisons to locate what continued to obstruct passage.
